"Why must it be said that it is not solitary?" The proponent of the established doctrine replied, "Because it is momentary." From beginningless cyclic existence, the momentary nature of this phenomenon, coexisting with its cooperative conditions, constitutes its first momentary instance. Therefore, its nature is definitively momentary. How could it become solitary?

If you think, "It still needs to be proven that a phenomenon occurring in a single moment produces a result," the text responds: "It has already been explained how it produces it." How something abiding for a single moment produces a result has already been explained above in the section concluding with, "because they neither existed before nor will exist after, and they are not of a different nature."

When this is the case, how could a functional thing endowed with capacity, which continuously produces a result and is characterized by occurring in a single moment, exist before, after, or differently? Because it has the nature of arising exclusively in a single moment, it is characterized by occurring in a single moment.

Some manuscripts read "characterized by occurring in *that* moment," which should be understood as: "Because it has the nature of arising exclusively in that specific intended moment, it is said to be characterized by occurring in that moment." Here, "before," "after," and "separately" are explained as terms indicating transformation into something else.

If you think, "It is clearly observed that seeds and so forth exist before they are aggregated, and exist separately and after when separated from the aggregate, which constitutes transformation into something else," the text responds with the passage beginning, "Whatever transforms..." That which has not yet aggregated, and that which is separated from the aggregate and isolated, is not the very phenomenon characterized by producing immediately.

Therefore, why would a momentary functional thing exclusively produce [a result], or why would the consequence be stated that it does not exclusively produce?

<summary>This section discusses the momentary nature of phenomena and causation, refuting objections about whether a momentary entity can produce results or exist in a solitary state before or after aggregation.</summary>
<keywords>momentariness, causation, cyclic existence, aggregation, functional thing, established doctrine</keywords>

The subject of the property is implied. Therefore, when it is said that the property of the subject to be proven is pervaded by one part of the thesis, it will be understood that it is pervaded by the property to be proven. If you ask, "Is not the subject also a part of that?", that is true, but it is impossible for it to be pervaded by it, because it is of the nature of a particular. If you ask, "Is it that pervasion is not understood in the particular, but it is not non-existent?", that is not so. Pervasion is of the nature of following and averting, and those are also of the nature of being present in all, and that is impossible in a particular. Therefore, the meaning of the statement, "The property of the subject to be proven being pervaded by the property to be proven is the reason," will be understood. Having explained "the property of the thesis being a part of it," in order to explain pervasion, the word "pervasion" is mentioned. Because the pervader pervades the pervaded, it is pervasion. Stating that is to state the particular nature of those individually ascertained. Therefore, whatever the particular of the pervader is like, that itself is stated as such; there is no "action" at all. Here, in the three phrases, the ascertainment to be grasped can be of three kinds: "only in that," "only in the pervader," and "only existing." Regarding that, since making the pervaded understood in order to make the pervader understood is tenable as being the making understood, it is shown that "pervasion by a part of that is the reason." Because the pervaded has following and averting in the pervader itself, and also as the reason making it understood, those themselves are the provers, this is shown. Therefore, when stating the nature of making understood, saying "because it is individually ascertained that if the prover exists, the probandum exists, the reason makes it understood," one should state "only existing in the pervader." If one grasps the ascertainment as "only the pervader exists," the property making it understood will not be shown, for the pervaded is present.

<summary>This passage elaborates on logical pervasion (vyapti), clarifying how the property of the subject to be proven is pervaded by the property to be proven, and distinguishes the nature of the pervader and the pervaded in logical reasoning.</summary>
<keywords>subject, property to be proven, thesis, pervasion, particular, reason, pervader, pervaded, probandum</keywords>

The non-deceptive state, devoid of harming factors, is the natural state. From what [is it known]? In a dream, it applies either to that very state or to another. "This is" refers to the enjoyment of intense delight. "For the purpose of knowing" implies that since at that very time one experiences it functioning for a purpose, it is non-deceptive. Therefore, waking and dreaming, through being non-deceptive and the alternative, correspond to valid cognition and its alternative; this is the meaning.

One might think that since seeing itself distinguishes between the true and the alternative in dreams and the alternative state, what need is there for another cause of distinction? Regarding this, "dreams and the alternative" means that merely appearing individually does not create the distinction between that state itself and the alternative, because there is no difference. The meaning is that the distinction between deceptive and the alternative is unestablished.

Is it not unreasonable to say, "Because a person has no apprehension of this?" The reason is that "because it does not exist" is not an apprehension, since saying "it does not exist" is an apprehension.

One might think that if there is separation from a support, no cognition whatsoever would arise. Regarding this, "the cognition of this as non-existent" implies apprehension by another, whether through direct perception or inference. Form, taste, and so forth are apprehended by direct perception which appears as them. Therefore, existence itself does not appear when separated from being isolated from others. Since it is precisely the essence isolated by that, it is known; even though it is not known by the subjects appropriate to it, it is known by itself. The mere essence separated from that is known by following direct perception, and is considered as the generator of the aspect of self. Therefore, the object of this apprehension is shown to be none other than what is considered: "having become such." That which arises from latent tendencies is also that distinction.

<summary>The text discusses the distinction between waking and dreaming states in terms of valid cognition and deception, emphasizing the role of apprehension and latent tendencies.</summary>
<keywords>non-deceptive state, dream, valid cognition, apprehension, direct perception, inference, latent tendencies</keywords>

By all who are not seers of the supreme. Those whose states are corrupted by what is to be grasped and the grasper, other than the Buddha; for only the Buddha knows that reality, and others do not. The Buddha, the Bhagavan, even though he has analyzed the very aspect of perversion, establishes it as it is seen. Thus, the cause of having attachment is taught. 

If it is not reasonable because it is not a seeing of the supreme, regarding the statement "grasped and" etc., those who are not seers of the supreme do not exist without the corruption of what is grasped and the grasper. Because they are constantly corrupted by the aspects of what is grasped and the grasper, such seeing and corruption are not supreme or specially exalted. 

If they also do not have the seeing of the supreme that is devoid of the two, by what will they know that reality? Because they have not uprooted the latencies of the two. Whenever they see what is devoid of the two, at that time they will see reality, because it has the characteristic of being devoid of these two. 

Therefore, those Buddhas, the Bhagavans, who are equanimous towards the object of reality, who have made equanimous that which is separated from the characteristic of the object of reality, having performed the elephant's gaze, like an elephant, even though they see the reality of objects, show as if they do not see it themselves. With only a worldly mind, they engage in external behavior. 

Having acted in accordance with the appearance that is strongly attached to the objects that appear to the world, they say, "Realize exactly as it appears! Do not hold on to what is opposite to how it appears!" Thus, regarding the establishment of the characteristics of external and internal entities...

It has already been shown that its existence is indeed that very nature. "Then how can a fire that does not produce smoke be fire itself, or how can smoke produced by smoke be smoke itself?" If this is asked, there is no such fault, because the specific characteristics of fire and smoke have been accepted in that way, but not merely fire. It refutes that what is not fire is the cause, but it is not accepted that all fire is the cause. Alternatively, it is not, because fire is not separated from the suitability to produce smoke, and from the beginning of its production, it does not depart from being the benefactor and the benefited, as has been shown elsewhere. 

If there is also a fire that does not produce smoke, is it not the case that mere fire is not the producer of smoke? Therefore, because this itself becomes a specific distinction like momentariness and so forth, would the specific characteristic change even if separated from fire itself, or alternatively, should it be stated in another way that smoke does not err from its cause, fire? If this is asked, the reply is: even though fire itself is endowed with specific characteristics, there are only those specific characteristics that have become its own essence. If it were not so, because fire itself is undifferentiated while the specific characteristics are differentiated, it would result in the acceptance of a universal. Therefore, just as fire itself makes them differentiated, similarly they are also differentiated by those that produce smoke and those that do not produce smoke, so there is no fault whatsoever. 

When the crown of Indra's head is of a nature that is not fire, at that time, if smoke arises from the crown of Indra's head, which is not the cause of smoke, it would become the cause, fire. If it is said that smoke does not err from fire because it does not arise from what is dissimilar, and because differentiated causes are what make things differentiated, and because that which produces smoke is the very aspect of fire, therefore smoke does not arise from what is not fire. Then how does smoke arise from dissimilar and differentiated cooperative conditions and from what is not fire? That very thing is stated: "Well then, now from differentiated cooperative conditions." They are dissimilar precisely by being differentiated, and are of a nature that is not fire. Thus, by the manner just explained, the result...

It should be connected as: "at that time, that very thing is also perceived as the cause of hatred and so forth." Because attachment and so forth are not certain with respect to bile and so forth, it is not all natures. And the particularity abiding in bile and so forth also becomes the nature of all particularities of attachment and so forth. Because the delusion is similar. Because it is so, the cause of the clear similarity of attachment and so forth is therefore. If one wonders how it is unreasonable, it is also said, "the particular transformation of phlegm and so forth." Even if any particularity of wind and so forth is the cause, all particularities will not be endowed with all attachments and so forth; because at all times a definite result is seen, it is to be inferred. The anticipation of the doubt "Because it possesses the cooperative condition of a definite particularity" is "However, the result..." Well then, that particular cooperative condition which is a definite cause is exactly familiarization; because from its divisions the divisions of attachment and so forth are seen. If another cause is imagined, then smoke also would not be established as having fire as its cause; the reply to this is "Which smoke without seeing fire..." Since smoke possesses fire, fire exists in that place; therefore fire itself is the cause of smoke, but the direction is not. If one thinks this, the doubt is "It is not..."

Otherwise, there would be no apprehension of a multihued object in paintings and the like. It is not the case that there is a single nature of a whole in paintings and the like. "If so, what is it?" There are various inherences of blue and so forth, and the apprehension of that is the apprehension of them. This is not the case. Thus, inherence is not multihued. "Why?" Because it lacks form. The nature of the quality of inherence does not have another quality called "form", because qualities do not possess qualities.

"Even if the object of the word is not the nature of multihued inherence, since it shares similarities with the various natures of the whole present in a multicolored butterfly and the like, it is explained by metaphorically designating it as multihued, just like something that is multihued." A mere designation is not the basis; it is applied to the so-called inherence. Inherence is not the object of a metaphorical designation.

If it is called multihued because it is similar to something multihued in that way, then in this way, there is no multicolored nature of a whole in a butterfly. There is not the slightest cause for metaphorically designating multihuedness in each individual part either. "If both are the causes for metaphorically designating different natures..." That is not the case, because there is no multihuedness in the form of a multicolored butterfly, and because there is no multihued nature in paintings and the like either. Furthermore, if it were a metaphorical designation due to inhering in a single meaning in paintings and the like, that too would be untenable.

If that is the case, whatever blue and so forth parts there are, if they have conjunction and inherence, there is no inherence of a multihued nature in each of those parts individually. Rather, the very nature of blue and so forth exists in them, because each individual one is not multihued. It is not reasonable to have a meaning that is merely designated, because there is no connection to a single meaning. "Even if that is the case, seeing the parts of blue and so forth in a painting and the like in sequence arises, and a multihued apprehension arises that synthesizes them, saying, 'That is a single multihued nature.'"

<summary>This page discusses the philosophical problem of perceiving a multihued object, such as a painting or a multicolored butterfly, and critiques the idea that such a perception arises from a singular whole or a metaphorical designation of multiple parts.</summary>
<keywords>whole, parts, inherence, multihued, perception, designation</keywords>

"whatever the essence of cessation is..." and so forth: Cessation is of two kinds: the essence of the stream being interrupted, and the characteristic of a dissimilar stream arising. Regarding this, if one speaks in terms of cessation as the essence of the stream being interrupted, that is illogical. Regarding the statement "that also does not exist at the end," since it is nonexistent by nature, how could one say "how could that also occur at the end?" Therefore, since this is not accepted to exist even occasionally, the consequence that it is a nonentity at the beginning and at the end is entirely disconnected. Likewise, regarding the arising that occurs through the connection of other moments of similar type in a lifetime, this is merely a negation; when a vase or the like ceases, the meaning is that that very thing does not arise, but it does not affirm anything in the slightest. If, however, one posits the second kind of cessation, which has the characteristic of dissimilar moments arising, that is not established as being without a cause, for it is explicitly accepted that it arises by the force of causes such as a hammer. For that very reason, it does not arise at the beginning, because its own causes, such as a hammer, are not present at that time. In order to establish the presentation of contradiction, it says "The entities of moments are of two kinds," and so forth: It becomes the cause for the sequential shrinking that generates moments of lesser, greater, and much lesser strength of only some entities, as, for example, cold and the like [act upon] fire and the like. Others, which are not like that, are not causes of diminution, as, for example, those very things like fire are for smoke and the like. Regarding those causes of shrinking taught first, although they have the nature of cause and effect, the world, whose appearance of knowledge is obscured by the darkness of ignorance, presumes them to be contradictory. "Many kinds" refers to the distinctions such as fire contradicting cold, wind [contradicting] a lamp, and darkness [contradicting] light. If one asks, "Should exclusion <term>apoha</term> not be accepted as the meaning of a word, because it obstructs that?" Therefore, it is stated, "That is not non-deceptive." "That" refers to words that are not exclusions, and so forth. "Is deceptive" means that because it does not make one non-deceived, it is deceptive, or because there is no non-deception in this, it is deceptive. 

Why is that? Because the connection with the real entity is impaired; because there is no connection with such a real entity, and because the real entity, which is the meaning of words defined by universals and so forth, has already been refuted. 

"If that is so, then how does awareness arise from words that are not exclusions of others, and so forth, with respect to the refuted meaning of words as exclusions?" It is stated: "All cognitions arising from words..." Some cognitions arising from words arise as an adherence to an unreal object, purely by the force of latent tendencies <term>vāsanā</term> from habituating to incorrect conceptualizations. Therefore, by the power of that, real entities do not become existent or nonexistent. 

Regarding what was said: "Of the word 'object of knowledge', etc...", it states: "the word 'object of knowledge', etc." To what does one state, "There is nothing to be excluded by words such as 'object of knowledge'"? First, if one asserts it based on words like "object of knowledge" that do not reside in a sentence, that are isolated and devoid of connection to other words, then it is establishing what is already established. This is because there is no application to the isolated, as it is meaningless. 

Showing that: In "Suddenly by the conceptualizing ones..." "Isolated" means connected with other words <note>The text likely implies disconnected, though phrased affirmatively here</note>. "Suddenly" means other than the context. Because the application of words by conceptualizing individuals is for the sake of benefiting the listener, not out of mere adherence. 

By applying to the isolated, it will not happen that the listener is benefited, which has the characteristic of reversing mere doubt and misconception. Thus, if the teacher does so for the sake of generating knowledge free of doubt after reversing the mind of doubt and misconception that has arisen in the listener regarding the isolated, in that case, this would have benefited them; but otherwise...

<summary>This section discusses the epistemological role of words as exclusions (apoha) rather than direct referents to real entities. It argues that isolated words without syntactic context do not convey meaningful exclusions or benefit the listener by dispelling doubt.</summary>
<keywords>apoha, exclusion, object of knowledge, valid cognition, epistemology, Pramana</keywords>

What if it is like grasping fire in fire? Grasping the common property of sharpness awakens the imprint of fire. Remembering that causes one to superimpose fire on the brahmin boy. Similarly, at the time of grasping one of the things like blue that were grasped sequentially, one superimposes what was grasped, and thus understands it as variegated.

If this is said, it is incorrect because:

When grasped sequentially, 
It is not mixed by the mind of multiplicity,
Because one does not grasp many.

If the reason for superimposition is similarity in sharpness, how is it superimposed here on the blue and so forth that is seen? 

If you say it is because of proximity, the grasping of proximity has understanding of grasping simultaneously, but not when grasping sequentially.

But if it is said that the word "certainly" is superfluous, it is because you <note>the opponents</note> establish the difference between the presence and absence of the sign in the similar and dissimilar instances. When the author of the treatise <note>Dignaga</note> says "only present in the similar instance and only absent in the dissimilar instance," others like the Naiyayikas establish a relationship based merely on seeing and not seeing. You establish it merely by that, and the word "because" points to that reason. To refute those opponents, the master <note>Dignaga</note> formulated the definition and correctly applied the word "certainly" (<term>nges pa</term>). We accept this. But if there is no misconception in others, it would not be applied at that time.

However, based on seeing and not seeing, they differentiate the similar and dissimilar instances by the objects of presence and absence. Even though a reason is seen to be present in a similar instance in some cases, and seen to be absent in a dissimilar instance in some cases, it is like the argument "He is dark, because he is the son of the dark one." Because there is doubt about the subsequent entailment and contraposition.

If so, subsequent entailment is the pervasion of the presence of the reason by the presence of the probandum in all cases. It is not necessarily established as contraposed without effort, so there is no contraposition. However, just as cold [arises] from fire at that time, at that time there is no trace called "latent tendency" distinct from the clear conceptualization of a non-entity, because it has the nature of that capacity.
